analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent commission to identify and recommend ending federal corporate subsidies and tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee favorably and was placed on the Senate calendar on August 27, 1996, but it never came up for a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an independent, temporary commission to review federal programs and tax laws that give payments, services, or tax advantages to for-profit businesses, and to identify ones that serve the industry rather than the public. Its recommendations would go to the President, and if approved, Congress would be required to introduce an implementing bill and vote on it under fast-track procedures with limited debate — the same model used for closing military bases. The goal was to end 'inequitable Federal subsidies': payments or tax breaks that give one company or industry an unfair advantage or windfall.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who the bill's findings say are unfairly forced to support subsidies that do not serve the public interest, and businesses that compete without federal support and today face rivals whose operations are propped up by federal payments or tax advantages.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares it 'unfair to force the United States taxpayer to support unnecessary subsidies, including tax advantages, that do not provide a substantial public benefit or serve the public interest' [S4].

The commission would review both spending programs and tax laws, flagging payments or tax advantages that predominantly serve a company's private interests, give one firm or industry an unfair competitive edge, or deliver windfalls [S2][S4].
Congress itself acknowledged it 'has been unable to evaluate methodically those Federal subsidies that are unfair and unnecessary,' which is why the bill creates a dedicated commission [S4].

Unlike an ordinary commission whose report gathers dust, approved recommendations would come to Congress as legislation that the Senate and House leaders must introduce within 14 days, with committees forced to act within 120 days and debate strictly limited [S4].

analysis.who_pays: If the commission's recommendations were approved by the President and Congress, corporations and industries receiving federal payments, services, or preferential tax treatment would lose that money. In practice, ending a subsidy means the industry's cost of doing business rises, which could show up in prices or jobs in the affected sectors.

drawbacks.text: The bill uses an expedited process that limits Senate debate to 30 hours, bars any amendment not germane to the bill, and bans motions to recommit — trading ordinary legislative deliberation for speed [S4].

The President can approve or disapprove only the entire package of commission recommendations, not individual items, and lawmakers would face an up-or-down choice shaped by an unelected commission rather than their own committee work [S4].

The definition of an 'inequitable Federal subsidy' exempts research and development awarded through merit-based competition, payments that primarily benefit public health, safety, the environment, or education, trade-obligation payments, and government procurement — carve-outs that leave a large share of federal support untouched [S4].

The commission only recommends; its findings still need presidential approval and a congressional vote, so a hostile Congress or President could stop the process simply by failing to act, as the bill's own failure-to-appoint and failure-to-submit deadlines acknowledge [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — an outside commission doing what Congress admits it cannot do for itself, namely identify corporate subsidies that no longer serve the public — addresses a real and long-standing taxpayer problem, and the expedited procedures are what give the recommendations teeth. The costs are real but standard for this model: an unelected body sets the agenda, debate is curtailed, and members vote on a package rather than each subsidy. The larger weakness is that the process is easy to strangle: the President must appoint commissioners on a deadline, and the process terminates itself if any step is skipped.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee approved the bill with an amendment and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of business, but Senate leadership never brought it to the floor, and it died there when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the bill on November 1, 1995, and it was referred to the Committee on Governmental Affairs [S6].
The committee held hearings on March 5, 1996, and on July 25, 1996 ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment [S6].
On August 27, 1996 the committee reported the bill to the Senate, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 567 [S6].
The committee's written report included additional and minority views, signaling disagreement among committee members even as the bill was reported favorably [S6].
No further floor action was taken before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries and corporations receiving federal subsidies and preferential tax treatment were better off, because those payments and tax advantages were never subjected to the termination review. Taxpayers got no savings, and the bipartisan push for a corporate-subsidy review went nowhere in this Congress.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed it through Senate hearings and committee consideration.

for.name: Sens. Fred Thompson and Dan Coats, and Sens. John Kerry, Russ Feingold, and Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from both parties.

for.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
for.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over government operations
for.what_they_did: Held hearings in March 1996, ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment in July 1996, and filed it with written Report No. 104-352.

for.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
for.role: Senator reporting the bill for the committee (R-AK)
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate on August 27, 1996 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, placing it on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; it sat on the Senate calendar for the final four months of the Congress and received no vote.

against.name: Committee members filing minority views
against.role: Minority of the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed additional and minority views on the committee report, registering their disagreement with the bill as reported.

against.name: Subsidized industries and their lobbying operations
against.role: Business sectors receiving federal payments and tax advantages
against.what_they_did: Opposed the corporate-subsidy termination approach during the 1990s corporate welfare debates.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Republican joined by two Republican and three Democratic cosponsors, and the Republican-led committee reported it favorably; the opposition that appears in the record is internal to the committee (minority views filed) rather than a party bloc vote.

industries.note: The commission would review federal programs that give direct payments, services, or benefits to for-profit businesses and recommend terminating those that serve private rather than public interests. These payments are costs borne by ordinary taxpayers for the benefit of specific firms.

industries.industry: Industries holding preferential federal tax provisions
industries.note: The bill explicitly covers the tax system, directing the commission to identify tax advantages that exceed what the law intended, favor one firm over similar ones, or disproportionately benefit one industry. Ending such breaks would raise these industries' taxes, offset by savings to taxpayers.
